title: India Signs Deal to Buy US-Made Javelin Anti-Tank Missile Systems
excerpt: The Indian Army will acquire the battle-tested fire-and-forget missile system under a deal that deepens a defense partnership unshaken by recent trade tensions between Washington and New Delhi.
body:
• The Indian Army signed an agreement to purchase FGM-148 Javelin anti-tank missile systems through the US Foreign Military Sales program, the US Embassy in India confirmed on Friday.
  • The package includes up to 100 Javelin rounds and 25 command launch units, following a $45.7 million approval by the Defense Security Cooperation Agency in November 2025.
  • US Ambassador Sergio Gor said the deal opens the door to co-production and strengthens both countries' defense industrial bases.

The Indian Army has signed an agreement with the United States to purchase Javelin anti-tank missile systems, the US Embassy in India announced on Friday, marking the latest addition to a growing roster of American weapons platforms in India's military inventory.

The deal, confirmed by US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, covers the FGM-148 Javelin — a shoulder-fired, medium-range guided missile system jointly produced by RTX and Lockheed Martin. The embassy did not disclose the financial terms of the agreement.

What India Is Buying

The agreement follows a formal approval by the US State Department in November 2025 for a potential sale valued at $45.7 million. According to the Defense Security Cooperation Agency (DSCA), India's requested package includes 100 FGM-148 Javelin rounds, 25 Javelin Lightweight Command Launch Units, basic skills trainers, missile simulation rounds, spare parts, lifecycle support, and technical assistance.

The Javelin purchase was part of a broader $93 million package that also included 216 M982A1 Excalibur precision-guided artillery projectiles, which India already uses with its M777 howitzer guns.

A Battle-Tested Weapon System

The FGM-148 Javelin is a man-portable, fire-and-forget anti-tank guided missile system designed to defeat armored vehicles, fortified positions, and other hardened targets. Its infrared seeker locks onto a target before launch, allowing the operator to immediately take cover or reposition — a critical advantage in combat.

The missile is known for its top-attack mode, following an inverted U-shaped trajectory to strike the roof of a tank, where armor is thinnest. It can also be fired from enclosed spaces like buildings or bunkers thanks to a soft-launch system that limits backblast. The Javelin gained widespread recognition for its effectiveness in Ukraine, where it became one of the most prominent Western weapons supplied to Kyiv's forces.

The system is already in service with the US Army and Marine Corps, as well as armed forces in over a dozen allied nations.

Gor Signals Co-Production Ambitions

"BIG news! India plans to buy the battle-tested Javelin anti-tank system. This is a great step forward in the U.S.-India defense relationship and opens the door to co-production possibilities."

— Sergio Gor, US Ambassador to India, on X

Gor said the agreement creates new opportunities for the defense industries of both countries to collaborate. "We see tremendous potential for future cooperation that strengthens the defence industrial bases of both countries," he said, adding that engagement between India and the US was at "record high levels."

The ambassador linked the purchase to broader strategic goals outlined by US Secretary of State Pete Hegseth at the May 2026 Shangri-La Dialogue, where Hegseth emphasized interoperability between the two nations' armed forces across land, sea, air, space, and cyberspace.

Defense Ties Hold Despite Trade Friction

The Javelin deal comes against the backdrop of strained trade relations between Washington and New Delhi. President Donald Trump doubled tariffs on Indian goods to 50% as punishment for India's purchases of Russian oil, souring the broader bilateral relationship in recent months.

Yet the defense partnership has remained largely insulated from that friction. India and the US signed a 10-year defense framework agreement in October 2025, and the Javelin purchase follows a re-order of General Electric F414 jet engines to power India's domestically produced Tejas light combat aircraft.

India's military inventory already includes a substantial American footprint: Apache and Chinook helicopters, C-17 Globemaster and C-130J Super Hercules transport aircraft, and P-8I Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft.

India's Anti-Armor Modernization

India is the world's fifth-largest military spender and the second-largest arms importer after Ukraine, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. The Javelin acquisition adds a modern anti-armor capability to the Indian Army's arsenal as it works to upgrade aging weapon systems along its borders with China and Pakistan.

The DSCA said the proposed sale would "improve India's capability to meet current and future threats by providing precision capability equipment, which will increase first strike accuracy in its brigades."

Officials on both sides have indicated the deal could pave the way for future co-production of defense equipment, a priority for New Delhi as it pushes its "Make in India" agenda in the defense sector. The Indian government was not immediately available for comment on the agreement.
nri_angle: The deepening India-US defense partnership strengthens strategic ties that benefit the broader Indian-American community and diaspora interests in both countries.
